Maladaptive Strategies.value: I push myself to exercise excessively
wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed

Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
There is something about me that made the event happen

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a male civilian-in-war-zone trauma profile, sexual objectification as a central trigger is not impossible, but in combination with the rest of the profile it lacks support from memory, threat, and appraisal items. The other items consistently describe war-related threat, distrust, flashbacks, and sensory trauma memory rather than sexualized threat, making this trigger hard to integrate into the same trauma presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: Water/flooding as a trigger is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the selected items. No memory, threat, or appraisal items reference water, drowning, environmental disaster, or any related theme. Given the otherwise interpersonal/war-threat profile, this trigger appears disconnected from the formulation.

issues.item: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not well aligned with the rest of the profile or the indexed trauma type. For a civilian in a war zone, water/flooding and alcohol smell are hard to reconcile with the threat, memory, and appraisal items unless there is some specific unreported trauma context linking them. The rest of the profile centers on generalized danger, distrust, flashbacks, and sensory recall, but these two triggers imply a different situational pattern that is not otherwise represented.

The maladaptive strategy set is partly disconnected from the rest of the formulation. Drug use is plausible as a broad coping strategy, but excessive exercise and concealing clothing suggest body-focused avoidance or managing visibility/safety in a specific way that is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items presented. Given the strong Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies and Threat → Maladaptive Strategies links, these strategies should plausibly follow from the reported triggers and threat beliefs, but these two items do not clearly do so.

vignette: Arjun was twenty when the mortar struck the courtyard where he and other expatriate volunteers had gathered. The blast collapsed the brick walls, and as he ran through the choking dust, he stepped over ruptured liquor bottles whose sharp, sweet odor clung to his jacket. Now working as a junior diplomat at the Washington consulate, the smell of alcohol and the memory of sudden, deafening bangs dictate his routine. When liquor drifts through the embassy’s glass reception halls, it immediately floods his system with dread. The odor of alcohol actively triggers a visceral threat response, forcing his pulse to race and his muscles to lock. Because the scent pulls him directly back into the chaos, it unlocks the fragmented, wordless horror of the event, leaving him paralyzed by memories he cannot articulate. The recall quickly warps his view of himself and the world, convincing him he was inherently foolish to be there and that life is fundamentally faithless. Because the trigger responses overwhelmed his nervous system, he quickly turned to taking drugs to numb the panic and pushing himself to exercise excessively to burn the adrenaline. This relentless sense of danger made it impossible for Arjun to trust that his embassy office was secure. The inability to trust safety meant his eyes tracked every stranger entering the building, reading ordinary greetings as attacks. The constant threat monitoring drained him, pushing him to rely on taking drugs and pushing himself to exercise excessively to cope. The threat of approaching figures immediately reignited his trauma recall, making his mind spin back to the courtyard. Because he could not articulate what happened, the vivid memories festered, deepening his loss of faith in people and certainty. The memory of his helplessness dictated his behavior; the clearer the image of the blast, the more urgently he braced for danger, making the memory itself a fresh trigger. The memory of the event also kept his sensory alarms chronically active; the more he saw the courtyard, the more readily the smell of alcohol and loud noises registered as imminent violence. The constant sense of danger kept his triggers chronically active; because his body remained locked in threat mode, the smell of alcohol and loud noises immediately registered as imminent violence. Arjun’s growing conviction that he was inherently at fault quickly dictated his conduct. Because he believed he was fundamentally flawed and that the world offered no security, he turned to concealing clothing to avoid being noticed. His deep-seated hopelessness pushed him to lock his emotions away, which intensified his perception that everyone was watching for his mistakes. The belief that he could never be safe also kept his triggers chronically primed; because he expected betrayal, any ordinary sound or scent immediately confirmed his dire predictions. The weight of these appraisals crushed his ability to engage with his partner, leaving him isolated and causing her to quietly retreat as their shared life grew tense. The maladaptive habits only fed the cycle. Taking drugs and wearing bulky, concealing sweaters in the consulate basement office left him exhausted and vulnerable to intrusive imagery. The compulsive exercise stripped away his mental defenses, making the vivid memories surface more frequently. As the drug use clouded his judgment and the concealing clothing restricted his movements, his body remained locked in high alert, interpreting every gesture as a precursor to harm. The strategies did not silence his fears; they amplified the sense that strangers were always closing in, even in his own apartment. Now, at twenty-four, Arjun stares at diplomatic cables he cannot focus on. The alcohol smell from a colleague’s spilled drink at a morning briefing still sends his heart racing, and the courtyard memory flashes before his eyes. He came to therapy because he is terrified he will lose his job and his partner will leave him if he never learns to quiet the alarms. He hopes, desperately, that someone might finally teach him how to stop running from his own life.
